name: Lower trap / serratus work
lead: Lower trapezius and serratus anterior work refers to exercises aimed at the muscles that control the shoulder blade (scapula). The lower trapezius pulls the scapula down and helps rotate it upward, while the serratus anterior pulls it forward around the rib cage; together with the upper trapezius they sustain upward rotation for overhead arm movement. [1][2]

In posture and looksmaxxing circles these muscles are discussed in connection with rounded shoulders and upper-back posture, with proponents saying that stronger scapular stabilisers support a more upright appearance. [3]

The encyclopedic sources describe anatomy and nerve-injury problems such as winged scapula, not trials of strengthening for posture or looks. No clinical study found tests the practice for appearance.

paras: The trapezius has upper, middle and lower fibres. The lower fibres arise from the lower thoracic vertebrae and depress and upwardly rotate the scapula, working with the serratus anterior and opposing the levator scapulae and rhomboids. [1]

The serratus anterior arises from the outer surfaces of the upper nine ribs and attaches along the inner border of the scapula, supplied by the long thoracic nerve. It protracts the scapula, nicknamed the boxer's muscle for its role in punching, and its lower part rotates the scapula so the arm can be raised. [2]

Damage to the long thoracic nerve is the most common cause of winged scapula, and the nerve is vulnerable in some surgeries such as axillary lymph node clearance. [2] Trapezius dysfunction can cause winged scapula and abnormal scapular movement, and accessory nerve palsy can cause shoulder drooping and pain. [1]

Exercises for these muscles are listed in posture routines for rounded shoulders and forward-head posture, alongside neck and thoracic work covered in related articles. [3] The anatomy articles loaded here describe no exercises.
No studies found on lower trap or serratus strengthening as a posture or appearance intervention in the sources loaded.

card.summary: Exercises for the shoulder-blade muscles used in posture routines; anatomy is well described, appearance benefit untested.
card.note: Sources cover anatomy and nerve injury, not training outcomes.

quick.overview:
The lower trapezius and serratus anterior steer the shoulder blade. Posture communities train them to counter rounded shoulders.

Anatomy sources describe their roles; no study found tests this training for posture or looks.
quick.mechanism: The lower trapezius depresses and rotates the scapula and the serratus anterior pulls it around the ribcage, together stabilising it during arm movement.
quick.risks: Low risk in general. Persistent winging or shoulder pain can reflect nerve injury and is a clinical matter.
